newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan police urge firms to confront racketeers.
newsitem.headline: Japan police urge firms to confront racketeers.

text.p: The chief of Japan's police on Tuesday urged business leaders to take a tough stand against racketeers, now at the centre of pay-off scandals involving some blue-chip financial firms.
"I want corporations to adopt a confrontational stance towards sokaiya (racketeers)," National Police Agency chief Yuko Sekiguchi told business leaders.
Sekiguchi's remarks came in his meeting with leaders of the powerful Keidanren business lobby, before the peak season of shareholders' meetings. The busiest day this year falls on June 27.
Public outrage has grew over suspected pay-offs to a racketeer that ensnared two of Japan's top financial firms -- Nomura Securities Co Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB).

The affair has already led to the arrest of more than a dozen top Nomura and DKB officials suspected of providing huge amounts of cash to a "sokaiya" racketeer for ensuring that shareholders' meetings proceeded smoothly.

Japan's Commercial Code bans payoffs to sokaiya, who extort money from firms by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings. But many firms have found it tough to cut the ties that bind them to the underworld.
Experts say that most companies bow to extortion threats and pay cash to keep their shareholders' meetings short and quiet and to avoid embarrassment.
A survey released on Sunday by the Mainichi Shimbun newspaper showed that nine in 10 Japanese companies said they had been threatened by sokaiya.
Japanese police plan to mobilise about 10,000 officers across the country on June 27 when more than 2,300 companies are to hold shareholders' meetings.
Most of the 2,300 firms have asked for police protection during their meetings, a police spokesman said.
As part of their collective strategy to avoid attempts by sokaiya to disrupt them, many Japanese companies have started to hold shareholders' meetings on the same day.
The number of sokaiya has been declining since 1982 when anti-racketeer laws were enforced.
But police believe there are still about 1,000 racketeers against the peak of nearly 7,000 in the early 1980s.
Raisuke Miyawaki, an expert on Japan's corporate culture and sokaiya, said banks and securities houses have been the main targets of racketeers, because of their desire to keep their images clean.
"Banks and brokerages serve as guarantees for racketeers that whatever crimes the sokaiya commit will never become public," Miyawaki told a recent news conference.
